This session I spent about 7 hours learning basic PCB design from scratch and doing most of the basics of this challenge

. I had never used KiCad before, so I started with a YouTube video (https://youtu.be/TvA4ut0o4bc?si=EgPMkzbhpzt4icdJ) and followed along to learn how a schematic turns into a board.

### My goal

My goal is to turn Starbie into a playable character shaped like a jet or a car, with its own page for viewing real-time stocks. I'm part of an investing club, so I want a little desk device that shows the market live and is also fun to play with at school and stuff.

### 1. Learning KiCad and sketching the schematic

I learned how the pieces fit together: a schematic describes what connects to what, then you assign footprints and turn it into a physical board. I sketched the schematic for Starbie Stocks. It has:

- the XIAO ESP32-C3 as the brain
- an OLED screen and an MPU6050 motion sensor on the same I2C lines (SDA and SCL)
- a DHT11 temperature sensor with a 10k pull-up resistor
- two buttons for changing screens and tickers
- power and ground symbols, plus no-connect flags on the pins I'm not using

I checked it with KiCad's Electrical Rules Checker. I fixed power-flag warnings and a footprint library naming problem before it came out clean.

### 2. Drawing the first PCB (the original rectangle)

Next I turned the schematic into a board and drew a plain rectangular outline. I placed the parts, routed the connections as tracks on the front and back layers, and added a ground fill on both sides. This took **a lot of trial and error**. KiCad's Design Rules Checker kept finding problems, including:

- a ground connection that was too weakly attached to its pad (a thermal relief problem)
- a ground via sitting too close to a pin's drill hole
- silkscreen text overlapping pads and the board edge

Each time, I changed the layout and ran the check again until only cosmetic silkscreen warnings were left and there were 0 unconnected pads.

### 3. Using Claude as a tutor for the error fixing

One of the errors was "thermal relief connection to zone incomplete" on a ground pad. I didn't know what it meant, so I asked Claude to explain it and used the explanation to fix the layout. A thermal relief is the set of thin spokes that connects a pad to a copper fill. Mine was connecting to a tiny isolated patch of fill, so the connection was too weak. I fixed it by changing how the tracks ran so the ground pad could reach the main fill, then re-ran the checker until the error went away. I handled the via-too-close-to-a-drill-hole error the same way.

### 4. Setting up my GitHub repository

I also set up the basic GitHub repo for the project, so everything is in one place and organized:

- a folder for the **code** (the Arduino sketch)
- a folder for the **PCB** (the KiCad project and the Gerber files)
- a folder for the **images** (schematic and PCB screenshots and renders)
- a **README** explaining the project, how it works and how to build it
- a **LICENSE**
- a **BOM** listing the parts and prices

### 5. What I learned

- How footprints, nets and tracks relate to the schematic
- Why clearance rules and drill spacing matter
- How to organize a hardware project so someone else can find everything
- That the first layout is rarely the final one. The rectangle doesn't fit the real, flat OLED and MPU6050 modules well, so I started redesigning it into a car-shaped board.

### Next

Next I want to finish the car-shaped board, export the Gerbers, add the BOM price sheet, and finish the code! :))))))))
